sections.heading: How to check text for AI
sections.body:
Start with the text you want to check. It can be an essay, a blog post, an email or one paragraph from a longer piece. Paste it into the box on this page, run the check, and wait a few seconds. The answer usually comes back in about 1 to 3 seconds.

1. Copy the text you want to check.
2. Paste it into the box on this page.
3. Run the check and wait a few seconds.
4. Read the AI likelihood line, then the three reasons under Why.

The result starts with one line: AI likelihood, a number from 0 to 100. Under it, the Why section lists three short reasons that point to specific phrases or patterns in your text. **Read the reasons first.** They show you what the estimate was based on, so you can judge the parts yourself. You can also copy the whole result with one click and save it with your notes.

sections.heading: What the score does and does not tell you
sections.body:
The score is a rough estimate of how likely it is that the text was written by AI. It is not a count of how much AI you used, and it cannot see how the text was made. A high number means the text has patterns that often show up in AI writing. A low number means it has fewer of them. Neither number proves anything about the person who wrote the text.

The estimate ends with a reminder: this is an estimate, and no detector is fully reliable. Keep that in mind when you read a high or low score. The number is a starting point for a closer look, not the answer.

sections.heading: Why no detector is fully reliable
sections.body:
OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, tried its own AI text classifier in 2023. It switched the classifier off on July 20, 2023, because its accuracy was too low. That is a useful sign of how hard this job is. A detector can flag human writing as AI, and it can miss text that an AI wrote. A single score cannot settle either problem.

For that reason, treat any score as one signal among several. A short text gives a detector less to work with, so its estimate is less steady. A long text gives more patterns to look at, but the estimate is still only an estimate.

sections.heading: Use the result as one signal
sections.body:
If you are checking your own writing, the reasons help most. Look at each phrase they name, and ask whether you would write it that way. Keep your drafts, notes and sources, because they show how the text came together.

If you are checking someone else's work, do not treat the score as a verdict. Read the reasons, ask to see drafts or notes, and talk through the text with the writer before you decide anything. A conversation with the writer will tell you more than a number can.

The check is free. You get 3 runs a day, and you get 3 more after you leave an email. You do not need an account to start. Each run returns the same kind of result: one AI likelihood line and three reasons.

sections.heading: Copy a Google Doc into the detector
sections.body:
Use these steps to check a document you have open in Google Docs.

1. Open the document in Google Docs.
2. Click in the text, then press Ctrl+A to select everything and Ctrl+C to copy. On a Mac, press Command+A, then Command+C.
3. Open the [AI detector](https://ai-detector.lazur.app/google-docs) in a new tab, paste the text into the box, and run the check.

Keep the doc open in another tab. That way you can compare the parts the reasons name with your own drafts and notes, without losing your place in the document.

sections.heading: Google Docs does not run the check for you
sections.body:
The detector is a separate web page, so it does not add a button inside Google Docs. You copy and paste each time. Copy the whole text when you can, so the reasons match the full piece you wrote.

If you check only part of a document, write down which part it was, along with the date. That way a result never gets mixed up with a different section or an older version later. A short note next to the result is enough, and it saves a lot of confusion when you come back to the doc a week later.

sections.heading: Check the version history
sections.body:
A score is weaker evidence than the document's own history. Google's help page says that to see version history, you click Last edit at the top right of the document, which is the version history icon. Hovering over Last edit shows who last updated the file and when they last made changes. Open version history to see who made which changes over time: [Google's version history guide](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/190843).

If a large block of text appears in one jump, with little editing before or after it, that is worth a closer look. It does not prove anything on its own, but it helps you see how the document was built.

sections.heading: Read the result for a document
sections.body:
The estimate covers only the text you pasted. A short section can give a different result from the full document, so keep track of what you checked. Read the three reasons, then compare each one with what you remember writing.

Free use is 3 runs a day, so plan your checks. Paste the full text in one go when you can, and save the result with your notes. If you use the reasons to revise your own writing, make the change in the way that suits your voice, and keep the draft you started from.

faq.q: Can teachers see if you use ChatGPT on Google Docs?
faq.a: This detector cannot see inside Google Docs. It only checks text you paste into it. Google Docs keeps a version history, which shows who edited a file and when, so it can show how a document was written over time. A teacher who wants to understand your process can also ask for drafts and talk through the work with you.

faq.q: How do I check if a doc is written by AI?
faq.a: Copy the text from the doc and paste it into the AI detector. Read the estimate from 0 to 100 and the three reasons. Then open the document's version history to see how it was written. The score is an estimate, not proof, so use both together before you decide anything.

sections.heading: Read the reasons line by line
sections.body:
The three reasons name specific phrases or patterns. Go to each one in the essay and ask three questions. Did you write it that way? Does the sentence say what you meant? Does a source support it? Those questions turn a vague score into a list of lines you can check.

If a reason points to a phrase you chose on purpose, note that in your draft notes. If it points to a sentence you do not remember writing, look at your earlier drafts and your research notes. The reasons help you review your own writing faster, and they show you where a reader might stop or slow down.

sections.heading: What a high score can and cannot show
sections.body:
A high score is a reason to look closer, not proof. No detector is fully reliable. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, switched off its own AI text classifier on July 20, 2023, because its accuracy was too low. A detector can flag an essay a person wrote, and it can miss text an AI wrote.

sections.heading: If you wrote the essay yourself

Keep the evidence that shows how the essay came together: the outline, early drafts, research notes and the list of sources. Those records are often more useful than a score when you need to explain your process.

Save a copy of your drafts somewhere you control, so you have them even if something changes later.

sections.heading: If your teacher asks about a score
sections.body:
Stay calm and answer with what you have. Show the outline, drafts, notes and sources, and explain how you researched and wrote the essay. Walk through the essay with the teacher and point to the lines the reasons named, so you can say why you wrote them that way.

The score is one input. A conversation about the work can show more than the number alone, because it shows how you think about your topic and your sources.

faq.q: Why does my essay score as AI when I wrote it?
faq.a: A detector looks at patterns in the words, so clear, formal and well-organized writing can look like AI writing to it. Read the three reasons and check whether they point to lines you wrote on purpose. Keep your drafts and notes, because they show how you wrote the essay.

faq.q: Is an AI detector accurate enough for school?
faq.a: Not on its own. OpenAI switched off its own AI text classifier in July 2023 because its accuracy was too low. A score from this checker is a rough estimate, and schools generally treat it as one piece of evidence beside drafts, outlines and a talk with the writer.

faq.q: What should I do if my essay is flagged?
